Sole
SOLE
n.
From Latin solea, a sandal or the bottom of the foot, from solum, the ground. Webster 1828: the bottom of the foot; the bottom of a shoe. Scripture uses it to mark the smallest possible measure of rest and the largest possible grant of territory.

Biblical Definition

The word measures the least amount of ground a creature needs, and Genesis uses it to say the flood had left none: the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot, and she returned unto him into the ark, for the waters were on the face of the whole earth (Genesis 8:9). The same figure becomes a covenant curse for a scattered people: among these nations shalt thou find no ease, neither shall the sole of thy foot have rest: but the LORD shall give thee there a trembling heart (Deuteronomy 28:65). Against these Joshua receives the promise in the opposite direction, where the sole of the foot measures possession rather than homelessness: Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given unto you, as I said unto Moses (Joshua 1:3). The grant is real and it is entered by walking. Isaiah uses the phrase to sweep a whole body in one clause and finds nothing sound in it: From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it; but wounds, and bruises, and putrifying sores (Isaiah 1:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SOLE as the bottom of the foot; and hence the bottom of a shoe, or the piece of leather which constitutes it; the foot itself.

expand to see more

SOLE, n. — The bottom of the foot; and by a figure, the foot itself.

The bottom of a shoe; or the piece of leather which constitutes the bottom.

The part of anything that forms its lower surface; as the sole of a plough.

SOLE, a. — Single; only; being or acting without another. (A distinct word, from Latin solus.)

Latin solea, a sandal, from solum, the ground or bottom.

Key Scripture

Genesis 8:9 — "But the dove found no rest for the sole of her foot, and she returned unto him into the ark, for the waters were on the face of the whole earth: then he put forth his hand, and took her, and pulled her in unto him into the ark."

Deuteronomy 28:65 — "And among these nations shalt thou find no ease, neither shall the sole of thy foot have rest: but the LORD shall give thee there a trembling heart, and failing of eyes, and sorrow of mind:"

Joshua 1:3 — "Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given unto you, as I said unto Moses."

Isaiah 1:6 — "From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it; but wounds, and bruises, and putrifying sores: they have not been closed, neither bound up, neither mollified with ointment."

Modern Corruption

Joshua 1:3 is a land grant to Israel under a specific covenant, and its routine use as a personal promise of territorial expansion detaches it from everything the chapter says.

expand to see more

Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given unto you is spoken to Joshua, about Canaan, with boundaries specified in the next verse, in fulfilment of a promise made to Moses. Its modern career as a personal warrant for claiming ground — territory, influence, markets — requires ignoring the boundaries, the covenant, and the addressee. The chapter’s own emphasis is the opposite of expansionist: what Joshua is told three times is to be strong and of a good courage, and the means given him is the book of the law, which he is to meditate in day and night that he may observe to do according to all that is written therein (Joshua 1:8). The promise is inseparable from the obedience it is attached to, and the possession is of a particular land God had named.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the way Scripture measures by the smallest unit. The dove could not find a foot’s width of rest; the scattered nation would not find a foot’s width of ease; Isaiah’s patient has no soundness in a single inch from sole to head. This is how the Bible states totality — not by abstraction but by naming the least part and denying it. The doctrine of total depravity is often heard as a claim that men are as bad as they could possibly be, which it does not mean; Isaiah 1:6 shows the actual sense, which is extent rather than degree. There is no part of the man — mind, will, affections, body — that the fall left untouched.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew kaph (H3709), the palm or hollow, used of the sole of the foot; regel (H7272), the foot; manoach (H4494), a resting place.

expand to see more

Hebrew kaph regel — the hollow of the foot, the sole; the phrase in Genesis 8:9, Deuteronomy 28:65 and Joshua 1:3.

Hebrew manoach (H4494) — a resting place; what the dove could not find (Genesis 8:9).

Hebrew darak (H1869) — to tread or march; the sole of your foot shall tread upon (Joshua 1:3).

Hebrew methom (H4974) — soundness, wholeness; what Isaiah finds nowhere in the body (Isaiah 1:6).

Hebrew ragaz (H7264) — to tremble or quiver; the trembling heart of the covenant curse (Deuteronomy 28:65).

Usage

"The dove found no rest for the sole of her foot (Genesis 8:9) — the least measure of ground, and there was none."

"Every place that the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given unto you (Joshua 1:3) — a real grant, entered by walking."

"From the sole of the foot even unto the head there is no soundness in it (Isaiah 1:6) — totality stated by naming the least part."
